origin_region: Yunnan · Xishuangbanna · Mengla · Xiangming · Yibang · Mansong
cultivar: Yibang small-leaf population (xiaoyezhong), old trees and newer replantings around Mansong
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, hand-rolled and sun-dried maocha, pressed into small cakes or sold loose; the tiny harvest is handled by hand from start to finish.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April); the old-tree spring harvest is the only one that justifies the name, though autumn small-tree tea is also sold.
appearance_dry: Small, slender, tightly twisted dark leaves with tiny buds, pressed loosely into small cakes.
appearance_liquor: Pale, almost champagne gold, perfectly clear.
appearance_wet: Small, fine, tender yellow-green leaves, the smallest leaf of any famous pu-erh.
taste_profile: Delicate and persistent: honey, orchid and a cool sugarcane sweetness, almost no bitterness, a light silky body and an aftertaste that keeps rising in the throat long after a steep; the price is for the finish, not the power.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, very briefly, and smell the lid. Small leaf, so use a touch less tea and flash the early steeps; porcelain only, and do not waste it on a distracted session.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and by tree class, and the class is the whole story: old-tree Mansong is a few hundred kilograms a year by most accounts and is sold in small lots and small cakes at prices rivalling Lao Ban Zhang and Bingdao, while 'small tree' Mansong from replantings since the 2000s is the only version most people will meet. The name was revived around the mid-2000s, so there is essentially no aged Mansong on the market and the few 2008–2015 old-tree lots are collector tea; what you can buy is young (1–5 years), 2015–2025, dry-stored. The year matters less than being sure of the trees.
description:
Mansong is a small village on the Yibang mountain in Mengla County, and in the Qing dynasty its tea was the tribute sent to the imperial court; the hill called Wangzishan, the Prince's Mountain, is the most famous of its gardens. That history and a tiny old-tree harvest make it, gram for gram, one of the most expensive teas in China.

The trees are the Yibang small-leaf type, growing in red soil at around 1,300–1,400 m, and most of the old gardens were lost in the twentieth century, so what remains is a scattering of ancient trees plus extensive replanting since the 2000s. Processing is careful hand work: light firing, gentle rolling, sun drying and loose pressing, because nobody wants to break a leaf that costs this much.

In the cup Mansong is quiet at first: honey, orchid and a cool sugarcane sweetness, a silky light body and almost no bitterness. What sets it apart is the finish, a sweetness that climbs in the throat and keeps going for minutes, and a session that stays clean and perfumed past twelve steeps. Brewed hard it tastes like nothing much, which is the usual disappointment of people who expect a famous tea to shout.

Sold by spring year and tree class, in small cakes and loose lots. The honest market distinction is between old-tree Mansong (minuscule quantity, eye-watering price) and small-tree Mansong (young plantings, still fine-leafed and fragrant, far cheaper); everything else labelled Mansong is a hopeful Yibang or an outright invention. Buy it only from someone who can say which trees and which year, and treat it as a taste rather than a stock.

If you want the character without the lottery, old-street Yibang gushu is the same family at a fraction of the price.
sources_note: The 'few hundred kilograms a year' figure for old-tree Mansong is a widely repeated trade estimate rather than an audited number; Qing tribute status is documented but details vary by source.
